title: O death, where is your sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the resurrection body: a seed goes into the ground, and something new comes up. Your line was sown, raised. Did a seed find some soil? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

For most of a long chapter, Paul has been arguing. Careful steps. If this, then that. Seeds and stars and the order of things. And then, near the end, the argument breaks open and he stops explaining. He turns, the way someone turns on a bully who has finally lost his grip, and he speaks straight to death. Not about death. To it. He calls it by name, the way you'd call out across a schoolyard, and he asks it a mocking question. It's short, and it's fierce. Its opening is today's word.

Here are the lines, in the King James words: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" First, it's borrowed. Paul is echoing the prophet Hosea, where the King James has God say: "O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction." Readers of Hosea argue over whether that line is a promise or a threat in its own chapter. Paul leaves no doubt: in his hands, it's a taunt. Second, the sting. The Greek word Paul uses can mean the stinger of an insect, or the sharp goad a farmer used to drive an ox. Either way, it's the point that does the damage. And Paul names that point: "The sting of death is sin." Some readers hear in that line that the hurt of death isn't only the ending. It's everything left broken, unforgiven, undone. Third, the turn to thanks: "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Paul isn't pretending people have stopped dying. He claims death has already lost, because of the resurrection he's spent the whole chapter on. Its point has been pulled. Fourth, the taunt ends in work. The very next verse says: "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord." Not a shout and then a nap. A shout, and then back to the job, because labor in the Lord is not in vain. Long after, the poet John Donne picked up the same nerve, writing a sonnet that tells Death not to be proud, and ends by saying that death itself shall die.
screen: `THE STING IS THE POINT THAT HURTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the verse to a fear. Settle, and breathe. Let one fear come up, about death, or about something smaller that feels like a little death: losing a job, losing a friend, getting old. Look at it squarely. Then, if you pray, you can say Paul's line to it, quietly: where is thy sting? If you don't pray, you can still ask the fear a question back instead of only listening to it. Notice whether it shrinks, even a little. The bell holds the time.
O death. The opening of Paul's taunt in First Corinthians fifteen, borrowed from Hosea: O death, where is thy sting?
Your line: where is your sting? Today, when a fear starts talking, answer it with that question, and then do one piece of good work it was keeping you from. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: 1 Corinthians 15 is read in the burial service of the Book of Common Prayer, and its taunt to death is sung in Handel's Messiah.

fork.setup: you're Paul. you've just taunted death: where is thy sting? what do you tell your readers next?
options: relax; nothing you do matters now.
be steadfast, keep working; your labor is not in vain.
go and look for death to prove you're not afraid.
fork.reveal: "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord." the taunt doesn't end in rest. it sends people back to work.

original.note: Greek: where, O death, is your sting? kentron is a stinger, or a farmer's goad.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about not being afraid to die.
what it means: Paul taunts death because Christ's resurrection has pulled its sting, and then sends his readers back to work.
what a scholar hears: kentron, a stinger or an ox goad, and an echo of Hosea 13:14, a line whose own sense is debated (promise or threat), reworked by Paul as a taunt.

notes: 1 Corinthians 15:56 continues 'and the strength of sin is the law'; only the first clause is quoted, to avoid a quick treatment of Paul and the law that could cast Jewish law as a foil. A Keeper may want the full verse.
κέντρον as both an insect's sting and an ox goad (cf. Acts 26:14); confirm. 'Long after' for Donne is a vague time word, not a date.
howItsDone mentions Handel's Messiah, which sets 1 Corinthians 15:55–56 as a duet; confirm. 'at funerals and on Easter' could be softened.
Original: ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ κέντρον; appears in both the Textus Receptus (first line, behind the KJV) and the critical text (second line, where 'grave' becomes 'death'); confirm accents.

Editor pass: 'Paul doesn't claim Christians won't die' sat awkwardly beside 15:51 ('we shall not all sleep'), so it now says Paul isn't pretending people have stopped dying (myth updated to match); the reading of 'the sting of death is sin' as everything left unforgiven is now marked as some readers' reading, not Paul's words; 'nothing done in love is wasted' brought back to the verse's 'in the Lord'; howItsDone narrowed to the BCP burial service and Messiah.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): the teach and trapdoor called Hosea 13:14 "an old promise"; in its chapter many scholars read it as a threat (the verse goes on "repentance shall be hid from mine eyes", and the Hebrew can be read as questions summoning death). Now says the sense is debated. Keeper: confirm.
